meta.title: WIPE — How Humans Wiped Before Toilet Paper
meta.format: Your Move long-form cinematic (evidence wall), picture-first, no-pause pacing
meta.tone: COMEDY LOCK (user, Nov 14, 2026): playful potty words throughout — poo poo, bum bum, buddy — silly euphemisms, straight facts. Advertiser-safe: no crude profanity.
meta.voice: same locked male AI Studio voice as CLIP; user generates

fact_notes: Toilet paper is recent: first commercial product 1857 (Gayetty) — 'barely 170 years old' is arithmetic from 1857 to today.
Stone Age kit (stones/leaves/moss/snow/water) is INFERENCE — organic materials rot; stated on screen with the INFERRED stamp, same honesty device as CLIP.

Greek pessoi: smooth stones/pebbles kept for wiping; the 'three stones' minimum is an attested ancient saying (widely cited in scholarship on ancient hygiene). Ostraka: pottery shards used for wiping; inscribed shards with names survive (archaeological reports, widely covered).
Roman tersorium: sponge on a stick in communal latrines, shared, rinsed in running water channel or vinegar/salt water (multiple museum/scholarly sources; the film says 'water channel').

China: paper used for toilet hygiene by 589 AD (Lapham's Quarterly timeline; DK/Smithsonian Inventions). Yan Zhitui (6th c.) advised against using paper bearing sages' writing as toilet paper — the paraphrase in L15 follows his Family Instructions. 1393 imperial order: 720,000 sheets for the court, incl. large soft perfumed sheets for the imperial family (recorded in Ming sources, via Joseph Needham, Science and Civilisation in China).
Medieval West: moss/hay/sticks common; wool/cloth for the wealthy; cloth fragments survive in cesspits (research report, Ireland/Norway finds).
Colonial America: dried corncobs by the outhouse; printed catalogues (Sears) and newspapers hung in outhouses afterwards (Farmers' Almanac and museum sources).

Gayetty 1857: first US commercial toilet paper, flat aloe 'medicated' sheets, each watermarked/printed with his name; sold as a health product; purchases were embarrassing/shame-wrapped (Smithsonian Magazine, 'A Brief History of Toilet Paper').

Scott brothers: toilet paper on a roll, 1890 (company history; they were initially embarrassed to be associated with it). Early paper could contain wood splinters; Northern Tissue advertised 'splinter-free' in 1935 (famous campaign, widely documented).
Close: most of the world uses water washing rather than paper (widely reported global practice; phrased without a hard percentage).

lines.text: So for thousands of years... how did everybody wipe their bum bum?

lines.text: The Greeks upgraded: little pebbles, kept by the potty.
